ground_truth.description: The old implementation used `project_root.glob('*/orchestrator.yaml')`, which discovered a config in ANY top-level directory, including one literally named `build`, `target`, `venv`, `node_modules`, etc. The new code prunes `_DISCOVERY_EXCLUDED_DIRS` at every level of the walk — including the root level — so a pre-existing top-level module directory whose name collides with a reserved name now has its `orchestrator.yaml` silently dropped. This is a backward-incompatible regression: such a module loses its overrides (test/lint commands, scheduling limits) with no error, which is a plausible cause of the observed escalation.

The recursive walk now discovers `orchestrator.yaml` at arbitrary depth anywhere under project_root, including files that were never intended as module configs (e.g. test fixtures under `orchestrator/tests/.../orchestrator.yaml`, vendored/copied trees not covered by the exclusion list, or nested config files). Any such file is registered as a module config with a deep prefix, producing spurious entries and triggering the depth>lock_depth warnings, whereas the old depth-1 glob could not pick these up.

`_first_component` still groups analytics by the top-level path component, but `for_module` now resolves configs by longest/deepest prefix. The docstring was edited to drop the 'matching how for_module dispatches' claim, acknowledging that analytics grouping no longer corresponds to actual config resolution; per-module analytics can now misattribute stats for modules configured at a deeper prefix (e.g. `foo/bar`).

This performs a full recursive `os.walk` of project_root on every call (startup via load_config and again inside run_full_verification), replacing a single-level glob. On large repositories with many non-excluded subtrees this is a notable, repeated cost, as the docstring's own performance note admits.

task.description: Extend `_discover_module_configs` in `orchestrator/src/orchestrator/config.py` (currently lines ~428-443) so it finds `orchestrator.yaml` files at any depth under the project root, not only one level deep. task.details:
## Why this matters

Surfaced by /review-briefing on know-live 2026-05-14. A downstream project now contains a nested orchestrator.yaml two levels deep declaring `test_command`, `lint_command`, `type_check_command`. Because `_discover_module_configs` only globs one level deep, those commands are silently NOT picked up by the harness today, even though the file is correctly authored and ready to be loaded.

The downstream orchestrator.yaml header documents the gap explicitly and uses absolute-cwd command form (`cd <subdir> && <command>`) so the same file becomes auto-discovered once this task lands — no downstream-side changes needed.

## Acceptance criteria

1. `_discover_module_configs` finds `orchestrator.yaml` at any depth (not just `project_root/*/orchestrator.yaml`).
2. Symlink-loop safety: walk with `followlinks=False` or track visited (st_dev, st_ino) to prevent infinite recursion. Add a unit test covering a self-referencing symlink cycle.
3. Standard exclusions still apply (no walking into `.git/`, `.venv/`, `node_modules/`, `.worktrees/`, `__pycache__/`, `build/`, `target/`, `.gradle/`).
4. Order is deterministic (sort by depth then lexically).
5. Backwards-compatible: existing one-level-deep nested orchestrator.yaml files still load identically.
6. Confirm by running on the downstream project where this was surfaced: the previously-undiscovered nested orchestrator.yaml is picked up and its commands appear in the verify pipeline.

## Cross-project reference

Surfaced as a known_gap in the downstream project's review briefing.
